name: Bioelectromagnetic therapy

card.summary: Bioelectromagnetic therapy is the use of magnetic or electromagnetic fields and devices for healing, which some people explore for recovery, skin and general wellbeing that shape how they look.
card.note: A broad category: some applications (bone-healing stimulators, TMS) are medical; consumer wellness devices vary widely.

quick.overview:
Bioelectromagnetic therapy is an umbrella term for treatments that apply magnetic, pulsed or radiofrequency fields to the body. It ranges from clinically used devices, such as stimulators for bone healing, to consumer products like magnetic wraps and pulsed-field mats.

People in appearance-focused circles approach it mainly through recovery and wellness: faster-feeling muscles and joints could mean more consistent training, and some devices are marketed for skin or hair. Research on the field of bioelectromagnetics is active, and findings differ greatly by technology.
quick.how: Practitioners and consumers use wearable magnets, pulsed electromagnetic field (PEMF) mats or pads, or clinic-based devices, usually for sessions of defined length. Clinical forms are delivered by clinicians; consumer devices are used at home, often alongside other recovery routines.
quick.risks: Radiofrequency heating is the best-established biological effect, and high-power sources and implanted medical devices carry documented hazards. Rapid-rate transcranial magnetic stimulation can heat electrodes and in severe cases burn skin. People with pacemakers or other implants are generally advised by manufacturers and clinicians to check compatibility first.

lead: Bioelectromagnetic therapy refers to the therapeutic use of electromagnetic fields on living tissue. It is a category used in complementary and alternative medicine overviews, which list it alongside practices such as biofeedback, acupuncture and massage [1]. The underlying science, bioelectromagnetics, studies how electromagnetic fields interact with living things, from cellular signals to man-made sources like mobile phones [2].

In appearance-oriented communities the interest is mostly indirect: proponents describe field-based devices as supporting recovery, comfort and general wellbeing, which they connect to more consistent training and a healthier-looking physique or complexion. Some consumer products are marketed more directly for skin or hair.

Within mainstream medicine, several field-based technologies are established or under study, including diathermy, bone-healing stimulation, transcranial magnetic stimulation and tumor treating fields, though experts disagree about how well some of them work [2].

chain: Magnetic or pulsed fields applied to body
Claimed easing of soreness and support of tissue repair
angle.text: Users apply field-emitting wraps, mats or devices around training or rest, hoping for quicker recovery or comfort. Any appearance payoff is reached through training consistency or general wellness rather than a direct change to the face or body.

infobox: Diathermy, TMS, bone-healing stimulation, PEMF devices, magnetic wraps
Listed among complementary and alternative medicine practices [1]

paras: Bioelectromagnetics covers fields produced by cells and organisms, effects of man-made sources, and therapeutic uses of electromagnetic energy [2]. Therapies in this family include radiofrequency diathermy, magnetic pulses used to stimulate parts of the brain, electromagnetic stimulation for bone healing and nerve stimulation, and alternating electric fields approved in some countries for certain tumors [2].

Heating is the best-established effect of radiofrequency fields, though biological effects at non-thermal exposures have also been reported and their mechanisms remain unclear [2]. Effects of low-power fields on human health are difficult to establish, and documented life-threatening effects are mostly confined to high-power sources and implanted medical devices [2]. The intermediate frequency range has been studied far less than extremely low and radiofrequency ranges [2]. The efficacy of tumor treating fields remains disputed among medical experts [2]. Exposure guidelines from bodies such as the International Commission on Non-Ionizing Radiation Protection aim to keep exposure at non-thermal levels [2].
Rapid-rate transcranial magnetic stimulation can heat metal EEG electrodes and in severe cases cause skin burns [2]. Diathermy heating effects range from muscle relaxation to burns [2].

No studies found on bioelectromagnetic therapy as an appearance treatment. Clinical research exists on individual technologies, such as stimulation for bone healing and transcranial magnetic stimulation, described in the encyclopedic overview of the field [2].
